title: EXecution-Eval: Can Language Models Execute Real-world Code?

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to evaluate LLMs' ability to execute code and predict program states, addressing issues with existing benchmarks being saturated or disconnected from real-world performance. Paper [4] explicitly mentions evaluating code reasoning capabilities, including predicting code execution behaviors such as program output and execution path, which aligns with the stated purpose. Paper [3] also critiques existing benchmarks for being insufficient and proposes a new evaluation framework for LLMs applied to code, but it does not specifically focus on program state prediction. Paper [6] discusses execution-based evaluation but focuses on code generation rather than program state prediction. Therefore, [4] is the closest match.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces the EXE benchmark, derived from 1,000 popular Python repositories and comprising 30,000+ tasks requiring models to execute code and predict final program states across diverse categories (e.g., math reasoning, logic inference, bit operations). Paper [4] mentions benchmarks for code reasoning, including predicting program output and execution path, which overlaps with the mechanism of requiring execution and state prediction. Paper [11] describes a framework for creating scalable execution-based benchmarks from natural code sources, which aligns with the mechanism of deriving tasks from repositories. Paper [6] discusses execution-based evaluation but focuses on code generation rather than diverse task categories or program state prediction. Thus, [4] and [11] both contain substantively equivalent mechanisms.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates using 33,875 test cases derived from 1,000 repositories, with metrics such as function call depth, identifier count, and task difficulty spanning simple to complex scenarios. Paper [4] evaluates code reasoning benchmarks but does not specify comparable metrics or repository-scale evaluation. Paper [11] describes scalable execution-based benchmarks but does not detail metrics or repository-level evaluation. Paper [3] critiques existing benchmarks and proposes a contamination-free evaluation framework but does not provide equivalent metrics or repository-scale evaluation. Paper [9] introduces RepoBench for repository-level code auto-completion but focuses on completion tasks rather than execution and state prediction. None of the prior papers match the evaluation design in terms of repository-scale metrics and task diversity.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM code understanding and execution evaluation. Papers [3], [4], [6], [9], [11], and [12] all work in the same general application area of evaluating LLMs for code-related tasks, including reasoning, execution, and repository-level understanding. While the specific benchmark instances differ, the domain is clearly covered by prior work.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to address four failure modes in code benchmarks: difficulty scaling, diversity, training data contamination, and low-cost scalability. Paper [1] discusses limitations in existing code benchmarks, including narrow programming language focus and task bias, which aligns with the purpose of improving benchmark diversity and scalability. Paper [5] explicitly addresses the issue of training data contamination in benchmarks and proposes methods to mitigate it, which matches the contamination-related aspect of the purpose. Paper [18] introduces scalable execution-based benchmarks to address limitations in existing benchmarks, including cost and diversity, which aligns with the scalability and diversity aspects of the purpose. Thus, the purpose is covered by [1], [5], and [18].

### Mechanism
The contribution's mechanism involves (a) filtering and preprocessing GitHub repositories, (b) generating diverse inputs for functions, (c) executing code to obtain ground truth, (d) constructing reasoning tasks requiring execution, and (e) leveraging typed function links for compositional task generation. Paper [8] describes cataloging GitHub repositories, which aligns with the filtering/preprocessing step. Paper [18] discusses creating execution-based benchmarks from naturally occurring code sources, which overlaps with executing code for ground truth and constructing reasoning tasks. Paper [9] introduces automatic task generation and verification strategies, which align with generating diverse inputs and compositional task generation. Paper [27] discusses systematic construction of benchmarks to measure compositional generalization, which aligns with the typed function linkage for generating complex tasks. Thus, the mechanism is covered by [8], [9], [18], and [27].

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates the benchmark's scalability (average generation cost of 1,123 tokens per case), reduced training-on-test risk, and statistical metrics like coefficient of variation (CV) for execution coverage and GPT-4 pass rates. Paper [18] evaluates scalable execution-based benchmarks, including cost and contamination risk, which matches the evaluation design. Paper [5] evaluates benchmarks for contamination risk, which aligns with the training-on-test risk aspect. Paper [27] evaluates compositional generalization using systematic benchmark construction, which aligns with the statistical metrics aspect. Thus, the evaluation design is covered by [5], [18], and [27].

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM code understanding and execution evaluation. Paper [1] explicitly focuses on evaluating LLMs for code understanding and generation, which matches the domain. Paper [3] introduces a benchmark for multilingual code reasoning, understanding, and execution, which aligns with the domain. Paper [18] focuses on execution-based benchmarks for code generation systems, which also matches the domain. Thus, the domain is covered by [1], [3], and [18].

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to empirically reveal the code execution capabilities of SOTA LLMs and identify the most challenging computational concepts. No prior paper explicitly reports or establishes the same empirical relationship between computational concepts (e.g., LOC, processing time, function calls) and pass@1 performance, nor does any prior work pinpoint specific coding features (e.g., floating-point multiplication, list slicing) as difficulty drivers. Papers like [1], [2], [4], [5], and [9] focus on evaluating LLMs on code-related tasks but do not empirically establish the same relationships or identify the hardest computational concepts. Papers such as [11], [13], [20], and [23] discuss code complexity or difficulty but do not address LLM performance or the specific computational features mentioned in this contribution.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves evaluating SOTA models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude3.5-Sonnet) and analyzing statistical relationships between task metrics (LOC, processing time, function calls) and pass@1 performance, as well as the influence of specific coding features. Papers like [11], [13], [20], and [23] analyze relationships between code metrics and difficulty or complexity, but they do not use the same mechanism of correlating these metrics with LLM pass@1 performance. Papers such as [1], [2], [4], [5], and [9] evaluate LLMs on code tasks but do not analyze statistical relationships between task metrics and performance in the same way. Thus, the mechanism appears uncovered.

The evaluation design includes relative model rankings (EXE vs. HumanEval), log-linear relationships between LOC/processing time/function calls and pass@1, and specific coding feature difficulty analysis. Papers like [1], [2], [4], [5], and [9] use similar evaluation designs, such as benchmarking LLMs on code tasks and comparing model rankings across benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval, MBPP). Papers such as [11], [13], [20], and [23] also analyze relationships between code metrics and difficulty, which aligns with the statistical framework used here. While the specific benchmarks and metrics differ, the evaluation design itself is covered.

### Domain
The domain is LLM code understanding and execution evaluation, specifically using code benchmarks. Papers like [1], [2], [4], [5], and [9] all operate in the same general application area of evaluating LLMs on code-related tasks.
